title: Conditional Expectation and Inequalities

intro.x: Conditioning is the central operation of probability: it is how information changes our estimates. This chapter extends conditional probability to random variables, proves the tower property and the law of total variance, shows that conditional expectation is the best predictor in mean square, and develops the standard inequalities (Markov, Chebyshev, Jensen, Chernoff, Hoeffding) that turn moments and transforms into probability bounds. It ends with symmetry arguments, which solve many problems with no computation at all.

sections.title: Conditional distributions and expectation: the discrete case

blocks.x: Let $X,Y$ be discrete. For $y$ with $p_Y(y)>0$ the conditional PMF of $X$ given $Y=y$ is
p_{X\given Y}(x\given y)=\Prob(X=x\given Y=y)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)} .
For fixed $y$ this is a PMF in $x$ (it is $\Prob(\cdot\given Y=y)$ restricted to $\{X=x\}$, a probability measure by Theorem 3.2).

For $y$ with $p_Y(y)>0$ define $\psi(y)=\Exp[X\given Y=y]=\sum_xx\,p_{X\given Y}(x\given y)$, provided the series converges absolutely. The random variable $\Exp[X\given Y]:=\psi(Y)$ is the conditional expectation of $X$ given $Y$.

The notation hides an important point: $\Exp[X\given Y=y]$ is a number (a function of $y$), while $\Exp[X\given Y]$ is a random variable (a function of $Y$), whose value changes as $Y$ changes. It is “the average of $X$ given what $Y$ tells us”.
Let $X$ be integrable. Then for every bounded function $g$,

\Exp\bigl[g(Y)\,X\bigr]=\Exp\bigl[g(Y)\,\Exp[X\given Y]\bigr].
\tag{$\ast$}
In particular (take $g\equiv1$), the tower property $\Exp\bigl[\Exp[X\given Y]\bigr]=\Exp[X]$.

\Exp[g(Y)X]=\sum_{x,y}g(y)\,x\,p_{X,Y}(x,y)=\sum_yg(y)p_Y(y)\sum_xx\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)}
=\sum_yg(y)\psi(y)p_Y(y)=\Exp[g(Y)\psi(Y)].
All rearrangements are justified by absolute convergence, because $g$ is bounded and $X$ is integrable.
Assume all expectations exist.
(Linearity) $\Exp[aX+bZ\given Y]=a\Exp[X\given Y]+b\Exp[Z\given Y]$.
(Monotonicity) If $X\le Z$ then $\Exp[X\given Y]\le\Exp[Z\given Y]$.
(Taking out what is known) $\Exp[h(Y)X\given Y]=h(Y)\Exp[X\given Y]$.
(Independence) If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, $\Exp[X\given Y]=\Exp[X]$.
(Total law) $\Exp[X]=\sum_y\Exp[X\given Y=y]\,\Prob(Y=y)$.

Each statement holds for each fixed value $Y=y$ because $\Exp[\,\cdot\given Y=y]$ is an ordinary expectation under the probability measure $\Prob(\cdot\given Y=y)$, so (i) and (ii) are linearity and monotonicity of expectation. (iii) Given $Y=y$ the factor $h(Y)=h(y)$ is a constant. (iv) $p_{X\given Y}(x\given y)=p_X(x)$ by independence. (v) is the tower property written out.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: the total law is the law of total probability in disguise

blocks.x: With $X=\indic_A$, we have $\Exp[X\given Y=y]=\Prob(A\given Y=y)$, and (v) becomes $\Prob(A)=\sum_y\Prob(A\given Y=y)\Prob(Y=y)$: Theorem 3.5.
Best prediction in mean square

blocks.name: Theorem
blocks.title: Conditional expectation is the best predictor

blocks.x: Let $\Exp[X^2]<\infty$. For every function $h$ with $\Exp[h(Y)^2]<\infty$,

\Exp\bigl[(X-h(Y))^2\bigr]=\Exp\bigl[(X-\psi(Y))^2\bigr]+\Exp\bigl[(\psi(Y)-h(Y))^2\bigr]
\ \ge\ \Exp\bigl[(X-\psi(Y))^2\bigr],
with equality iff $h(Y)=\psi(Y)$ almost surely. So $\psi(Y)=\Exp[X\given Y]$ is the function of $Y$ minimising mean squared error.

Write $X-h(Y)=(X-\psi(Y))+(\psi(Y)-h(Y))$ and expand the square. The cross term is $2\Exp[(X-\psi(Y))\,g(Y)]$ with $g=\psi-h$; by the defining property $(\ast)$, $\Exp[g(Y)X]=\Exp[g(Y)\psi(Y)]$, so the cross term vanishes. (Boundedness of $g$ in $(\ast)$ is removed by a limiting argument using $\Exp[g(Y)^2]<\infty$; see Chapter 15.)

Geometrically, $X-\Exp[X\given Y]$ is “orthogonal” to every function of $Y$, and $\Exp[X\given Y]$ is the orthogonal projection of $X$ onto the space of functions of $Y$. This viewpoint is the key to the abstract definition in Chapter 15.
The law of total variance
Define the conditional variance $\Var(X\given Y)=\Exp\bigl[(X-\psi(Y))^2\given Y\bigr]$.
If $\Exp[X^2]<\infty$,
\Var(X)=\Exp\bigl[\Var(X\given Y)\bigr]+\Var\bigl(\Exp[X\given Y]\bigr).

Write $X-\mu=(X-\psi(Y))+(\psi(Y)-\mu)$ where $\mu=\Exp[X]=\Exp[\psi(Y)]$. Square and take expectations. The cross term $2\Exp[(X-\psi(Y))(\psi(Y)-\mu)]$ is zero by $(\ast)$ with $g=\psi-\mu$. The first square has expectation $\Exp[\Exp[(X-\psi(Y))^2\given Y]]=\Exp[\Var(X\given Y)]$ by the tower property, and the second is $\Var(\psi(Y))$.
The two terms are the unexplained variance (average spread of $X$ around its prediction) and the explained variance (spread of the prediction itself).

Let $S=\sum_{i=1}^NX_i$ with $X_i$ i.i.d. (mean $\mu$, variance $\sigma^2$), $N$ independent of the $X_i$. Given $N=n$, $\Exp[S\given N]=N\mu$ and $\Var(S\given N)=N\sigma^2$. The tower property and the law of total variance give
\Exp[S]=\mu\Exp[N],\qquad\Var(S)=\sigma^2\Exp[N]+\mu^2\Var(N),
exactly as in Theorem 9.9, with no generating functions.
If $(X,Y)$ has joint density $f$, the conditional density of $X$ given $Y=y$ is
f_{X\given Y}(x\given y)=\frac{f(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},\qquad f_Y(y)>0,

and $\Exp[X\given Y=y]=\int xf_{X\given Y}(x\given y)\,dx$. The defining property $(\ast)$, the tower property, the total variance formula and Theorems 10.3 and 10.4 hold with the same proofs, with sums replaced by integrals (the interchange of integrals is justified by Fubini’s theorem, Chapter 15). Example: for the bivariate normal, Theorem 8.18(ii) gives $\Exp[Y\given X]=\rho X$ and $\Var(Y\given X)=1-\rho^2$, and the total variance formula recovers $\Var(Y)=(1-\rho^2)+\rho^2=1$.

blocks.name: Nuance
blocks.title: conditioning on a probability-zero event is a definition, not a theorem

blocks.x: For continuous $Y$ we condition on $\{Y=y\}$, which has probability zero, so $\Prob(A\given Y=y)=\Prob(A\cap\{Y=y\})/\Prob(Y=y)$ is $0/0$. What we have defined is a function $\psi(y)$ that satisfies $(\ast)$; it is determined only up to a set of $y$ of probability zero, and its value at any single point is arbitrary. It also depends on how the null event is approached. Take a point uniformly distributed on a sphere and condition on “the point lies on a given great circle”. If the circle is regarded as the equator (condition on latitude $=0$), the position along it is uniformly distributed. If the same kind of circle is regarded as a meridian (condition on longitude fixed), the conditional density of the latitude along it is proportional to the cosine of the latitude, which is not uniform. The same geometric set gets different conditional distributions depending on the variable being conditioned on. This is the Borel–Kolmogorov paradox. The remedy is always to specify the conditioning variable, not just the event.
The law of total expectation turns hard problems into linear equations: condition on the outcome of the first step, and use the fact that the process restarts.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Expected waiting time for HH and for HT

blocks.x: A fair coin is tossed until a given pattern appears. Let $E$ be the expected number of tosses. For HH: define states “start” ($E_0$) and “last toss was H” ($E_1$). From the start, one toss is made; heads moves to state $1$, tails stays at the start: $E_0=1+\tfrac12E_1+\tfrac12E_0$. From state $1$: heads ends the game, tails returns to start: $E_1=1+\tfrac12\cdot0+\tfrac12E_0$. Substituting, $E_0=1+\tfrac12(1+\tfrac12E_0)+\tfrac12E_0=\tfrac32+\tfrac34E_0$, so $E_0=6$.

For HT: $E_0=1+\tfrac12E_1+\tfrac12E_0$ as before, but from state $1$, heads keeps us in state $1$ and tails ends: $E_1=1+\tfrac12E_1$, so $E_1=2$ and $E_0=1+1+\tfrac12E_0$ gives $E_0=4$. The two patterns are equally likely in any fixed window of tosses, yet HH takes longer on average: HH can overlap itself, so its occurrences come in clumps, and the clumping increases the wait for the first occurrence.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Waiting for $n$ heads in a row

blocks.x: Let $E_n$ be the expected number of tosses to get $n$ consecutive heads. To get $n$ in a row we first need $n-1$ in a row (expected $E_{n-1}$ tosses), then one more toss: heads (probability $\tfrac12$) completes the run; tails (probability $\tfrac12$) sends us back to the start. Hence

E_n=E_{n-1}+1+\tfrac12\cdot0+\tfrac12E_n\ \Longrightarrow\ E_n=2E_{n-1}+2,
\qquad E_0=0,
and by induction $E_n=2^{n+1}-2$. For $n=2$ we get $6$, matching the previous example.

Whenever a process regenerates (coin sequences, random walks, dice-until-condition), set up one equation per state: $E_s=1+\sum_{s'}\Prob(s\to s')E_{s'}$, with $E=0$ at absorbing targets, and solve the linear system. We return to this systematically for Markov chains in Chapter 12.
If $X\ge0$ and $a>0$, then $\Prob(X\ge a)\le\Exp[X]/a$.
Pointwise, $a\indic_{\{X\ge a\}}\le X$ (if $X\ge a$ the left is $a\le X$; otherwise it is $0\le X$). Take expectations: $a\Prob(X\ge a)\le\Exp[X]$.
If $\Exp[X^2]<\infty$ and $t>0$, then $\Prob(\abs{X-\mu}\ge t)\le\sigma^2/t^2$.
Apply Markov to the non-negative variable $(X-\mu)^2$ and the level $t^2$.

Chebyshev says that at least $1-1/k^2$ of the mass lies within $k$ standard deviations of the mean, for any distribution with finite variance. It is crude (for the normal the actual probability beyond $2\sigma$ is $0.046$, versus the bound $0.25$) but universal.
For $t>0$, $\Prob(X-\mu\ge t)\le\dfrac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+t^2}$.
For any $u\ge0$, $\{X-\mu\ge t\}\subseteq\{(X-\mu+u)^2\ge(t+u)^2\}$, so by Markov
\Prob(X-\mu\ge t)\le\frac{\Exp[(X-\mu+u)^2]}{(t+u)^2}=\frac{\sigma^2+u^2}{(t+u)^2}.
Choose $u=\sigma^2/t$ (which minimises the right side): the bound becomes $\dfrac{\sigma^2+\sigma^4/t^2}{(t+\sigma^2/t)^2}=\dfrac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+t^2}$.
If $\varphi:\R\to\R$ is convex and $X$, $\varphi(X)$ are integrable, then $\varphi(\Exp[X])\le\Exp[\varphi(X)]$. If $\varphi$ is strictly convex, equality holds iff $X$ is almost surely constant.

A convex function has a supporting line at every point: with $\mu=\Exp[X]$ there is a constant $c$ (a subgradient at $\mu$) such that $\varphi(x)\ge\varphi(\mu)+c(x-\mu)$ for all $x$. Substitute $x=X$ and take expectations: $\Exp[\varphi(X)]\ge\varphi(\mu)+c\cdot0=\varphi(\mu)$. For strictly convex $\varphi$ the supporting line touches the graph only at $\mu$, so equality forces $X=\mu$ almost surely.
$\varphi(x)=x^2$: $(\Exp[X])^2\le\Exp[X^2]$, i.e. $\Var(X)\ge0$.
$\varphi(x)=\abs x^p$, $p\ge1$: $\bigl(\Exp\abs X\bigr)^p\le\Exp\abs X^p$, so $\norm{X}_r=(\Exp\abs X^r)^{1/r}$ is non-decreasing in $r\ge1$.
$\varphi(x)=-\ln x$ for $X>0$: $\Exp[\ln X]\le\ln\Exp[X]$, the AM–GM inequality for expectations.
$\varphi(x)=e^{tx}$: $M_X(t)\ge e^{t\Exp[X]}$.

blocks.name: Common pitfall
blocks.title: Jensen reverses for concave functions, and $\Exp[1/X]\ne1/\Exp[X]$

blocks.x: For concave $\varphi$ the inequality reverses. For instance $\Exp[1/X]\ge1/\Exp[X]$ for $X>0$ (since $1/x$ is convex). A common error in finance and queueing is to replace $\Exp[g(X)]$ by $g(\Exp[X])$; Jensen shows the sign of the error.
Chebyshev’s polynomial tail $1/t^2$ is too weak for sums of many independent variables. Applying Markov to an exponential gives far sharper bounds.
For every $a$ and every $t>0$ in the domain of the MGF,

\Prob(X\ge a)\le e^{-ta}M_X(t),\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\Prob(X\ge a)\le\inf_{t>0}e^{-ta}M_X(t).
$\{X\ge a\}=\{e^{tX}\ge e^{ta}\}$ since $e^{tx}$ is increasing; apply Markov to the non-negative variable $e^{tX}$.
For $Z\sim N(0,1)$, $e^{-ta}M(t)=e^{-ta+t^2/2}$ is minimised at $t=a$, giving $\Prob(Z\ge a)\le e^{-a^2/2}$ for $a>0$.

Let $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ and $\alpha\in(p,1)$. Then $e^{-t\alpha n}M_X(t)= \exp\bigl(n[-t\alpha+\ln(q+pe^t)]\bigr)$. Setting the derivative of the bracket to zero, $-\alpha+pe^t/(q+pe^t)=0$, gives $e^t=\alpha q/((1-\alpha)p)$, and then $q+pe^t=q/(1-\alpha)$. Substituting,
-t\alpha+\ln(q+pe^t)=-\alpha\ln\frac\alpha p-(1-\alpha)\ln\frac{1-\alpha}q=-D(\alpha\|p),
where $D(\alpha\|p)=\alpha\ln\frac\alpha p+(1-\alpha)\ln\frac{1-\alpha}{1-p}\ge0$ is the relative entropy (Kullback–Leibler divergence) between Bernoulli laws. Hence
\Prob(X\ge\alpha n)\le e^{-nD(\alpha\|p)}.
The tail probability decays exponentially in $n$, with rate given by $D$. (Cram'er’s theorem says this rate is exact to first order.)
If $\Exp[X]=0$ and $a\le X\le b$ almost surely, then for every real $s$, $\Exp[e^{sX}]\le\exp\bigl(s^2(b-a)^2/8\bigr)$.
Note $a\le0\le b$. By convexity of $x\mapsto e^{sx}$, for $x\in[a,b]$, $e^{sx}\le\frac{b-x}{b-a}e^{sa}+\frac{x-a}{b-a}e^{sb}$. Taking expectations and using $\Exp[X]=0$:
\Exp[e^{sX}]\le\frac{b\,e^{sa}-a\,e^{sb}}{b-a}.
Set $p=-a/(b-a)\in[0,1]$ and $u=s(b-a)$. Then the right side equals $e^{-pu}(1-p+pe^u)=e^{L(u)}$ where $L(u)=-pu+\ln(1-p+pe^u)$. We have $L(0)=0$, $L'(u)=-p+\dfrac{pe^u}{1-p+pe^u}$ so $L'(0)=0$, and
L''(u)=r(1-r),\qquad r=\frac{pe^u}{1-p+pe^u}\in[0,1],
so $L''(u)\le\tfrac14$ for all $u$. By Taylor’s theorem with Lagrange remainder, $L(u)=L(0)+L'(0)u+\tfrac12L''(\xi)u^2\le u^2/8=s^2(b-a)^2/8$.
Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent with $a_i\le X_i\le b_i$, and $S_n=\sum X_i$. Then for every $t>0$,
\Prob\bigl(S_n-\Exp[S_n]\ge t\bigr)\le\exp\Bigl(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_i(b_i-a_i)^2}\Bigr),
and the same bound holds for $\Prob(S_n-\Exp[S_n]\le-t)$; the two-sided probability is at most twice the bound.
By the Chernoff method with parameter $s>0$, independence, and Lemma 10.17 applied to $X_i-\Exp[X_i]$ (which lies in an interval of length $b_i-a_i$ and has mean zero),

\Prob(S_n-\Exp[S_n]\ge t)\le e^{-st}\prod_i\Exp\bigl[e^{s(X_i-\Exp X_i)}\bigr]
\le\exp\Bigl(-st+\frac{s^2}8\sum_i(b_i-a_i)^2\Bigr).
The exponent is minimised at $s=4t/\sum(b_i-a_i)^2$, giving $-2t^2/\sum(b_i-a_i)^2$.

Let $X_i\in\{0,1\}$ be i.i.d. Bernoulli$(p)$ answers and $\hat p=S_n/n$. Then $\Prob(\abs{\hat p-p}\ge\epsilon)\le2e^{-2n\epsilon^2}$. For accuracy $\epsilon=0.03$ with failure probability at most $5\%$ we need $2e^{-2n(0.0009)}\le0.05$, i.e. $n\ge\ln(40)/(0.0018)\approx2050$ samples (no dependence on $p$).
Random variables $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are exchangeable if $(X_{\pi(1)},\dots,X_{\pi(n)})$ has the same joint distribution as $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ for every permutation $\pi$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$.

I.i.d. variables are exchangeable. So are the successive draws from an urn without replacement: the probability of any specific sequence of colours is $\frac{K(K-1)\cdots}{N(N-1)\cdots}$, a product of numerators that depends only on how many of each colour appear, not on their order.

blocks.name: Interview check
blocks.title: symmetry solves many problems without computation

blocks.x: If $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are exchangeable, then each $X_i$ has the same distribution, each pair $(X_i,X_j)$ the same joint law, and so on. Example: a card dealt second from a shuffled deck is an ace with probability $4/52$, the same as the first. Example (aces before kings): in a shuffled deck, what is the probability that the first ace comes before the first king? Look only at the relative order of the $8$ cards that are aces or kings. By exchangeability the first of these $8$ is equally likely to be any of them, so it is an ace with probability $4/8=\tfrac12$. All the other cards are irrelevant.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Expected number of cards before the first ace

blocks.x: The $4$ aces split the other $48$ cards into $5$ groups (before the first ace, between, and after the last). By symmetry each of the $48$ cards is equally likely to fall in each of the $5$ groups, so the expected size of the first group is $48/5=9.6$, and the first ace is on average at position $9.6+1=10.6$.
Roll a die and let $N$ be the result; then toss $N$ fair coins. Find $\Exp[H\given N]$, $\Exp[H]$ and $\Var(H)$, where $H$ is the number of heads.
Show $\Var(X)=\Exp[\Var(X\given Y)]+\Var(\Exp[X\given Y])$ in the example where $Y$ is a fair coin and $X\given Y\sim N(\pm1,1)$.
Find the expected number of tosses to get TTH, HTH, and HHH. Which is largest?
Use Markov’s inequality to show $\Prob(X\ge10)\le0.1$ if $X\ge0$ and $\Exp[X]=1$, and show the bound can be attained.
Show that for a random variable with mean $0$ and variance $1$, $\Prob(X\ge t)\le\frac1{1+t^2}$ and that this is attained for some distribution.
(Paley–Zygmund) Prove $\Prob(X>\theta\Exp[X])\ge(1-\theta)^2\frac{(\Exp X)^2}{\Exp[X^2]}$ for $X\ge0$ and $0<\theta<1$. (Hint: Cauchy–Schwarz applied to $X\indic_{\{X>\theta\Exp X\}}$.)
$n$ fair coins are tossed. Using Hoeffding, bound the probability that the number of heads exceeds $n/2+\sqrt{n\ln n}$.
A deck is shuffled. Find the expected number of cards strictly between the first ace and the second ace. (Symmetry.)
(Challenge) Prove that if $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are exchangeable with $\Exp[X_1^2]<\infty$, then $\Cov(X_1,X_2)\ge-\Var(X_1)/(n-1)$. (Hint: compute $\Var(\sum X_i)\ge0$.)
